toc.title: Calm and regulation are not the same thing
Calm on the outside, chaos on the inside
Why we can't sit with discomfort

blocks.p: These are questions people brought me, and the conversation covered a lot: the difference between calm and regulation, faking safety, the Will Smith moment at the Oscars, what shame is and what it's for, time-outs, and why we have such a hard time sitting with discomfort.

blocks.h: Calm and regulation are not the same thing

blocks.p: Someone asked me how to tell the difference between calming and regulating. I don't know if I've ever explicitly separated them. It really depends on what we mean by calm and by regulation.

When I say calm, it could be a behavioral thing, where physically we exude calmness. Not lethargy, where we're worn out and blah, but calm. I can have energy and still be calm. I'm not fully relaxed, I'm not in solitude, at peace, meditating, but I'm calm. Physically, behaviorally, even in my voice, I have enough vocal prosody.

When I say regulation, I think of the state of my autonomic nervous system. So even though I exude and feel and behave calm, am I truly in a ventral vagal state? I might feel like I am, but I might also have some flight activation, a little bit of anxiety in my system. I'm behaviorally calm, and inwardly I feel mostly calm, but I feel a little bit of energy in my system at the same time, which I wouldn't call calm.

Being regulated is not a feeling. We're talking about your autonomic nervous system. We're talking about biology. Being regulated means your safe and social pathways, the ventral vagal pathways, are activated enough for you to be able to socially engage, to cope, to ground yourself, to feel in the present moment enough. It doesn't have to be 100%.

One causes the other. If you're regulated, anchored enough in your safety state, then the behavior that follows can be stillness, being able to be still. The feeling that follows could be calm. It could also be playful, happy, joyful, relaxed. It could be a bunch of things. Calm is one of the feelings or behaviors that can follow a well-regulated state. So I would say calm is the sensation of being regulated.

blocks.h: Calm on the outside, chaos on the inside

blocks.p: The follow-up question was a good one: what about people who are chronically activated, where the behavior appears calm but it's chaos on the inside? One person, a teacher, said that for him, presenting calm while activated was survival when he was younger, and professionally it's survival now too.

Biologically, I can only speculate. To me, that means there's enough of the safety state active to do what I'll just call self-control. That's not really self-regulation. That's just white-knuckling it.

Self-regulation would be: I feel dysregulated, I feel more flight or fight energy, and then I can work my way up my [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) into my safety state and actually feel feelings of calm. That I would call self-regulation. But if we're activated, if we're having a panic attack or something like that, and we're just getting through it, self-control might be the best word for that. And self-control is better than nothing, depending on what it is.
The person who asked said that even when she touches the safe and social state, she's always looking down the ladder, waiting for what's going to happen next.

That speaks to something else. When we do get to safety, when we truly get to the top of the ladder, it might just be a little glimpse. Deb Dana calls it a glimmer. It's just a moment, but all of a sudden things might feel different.

With my clients, especially the students I worked with at the time, they'd have those moments where they're connecting and smiling and all of a sudden making eye contact. But it feels weird. It feels uncomfortable. It feels like vulnerability. It is vulnerability, but to them it's not experienced as safe vulnerability. It's probably experienced more as unsafe exposure.
What about when it's contrived? You learn to present a certain way, forcing the appearance of safe and social, even though you're feeling something else.

Then it's not truly a reflection of your safe and social state. It's an adaptation, maybe to get a need met, for some people. Other people, who are in a truly dysregulated state, can use a pseudo safety state, a faux safety state, to get their selfish needs met, to manipulate others. That does not come from an empathetic safety state. I would assume that comes from more of a fight state, or a rageful freeze kind of thing.
So maybe we can lump the ways we fake it, the ways we adapt and present ourselves, into two groups:

ul: I'm getting my needs met, and I have to survive.
I'm getting my selfish wants met, and I'm exploiting others.

blocks.p: And I think those two people oftentimes find each other, unfortunately. Someone said that sounded like narcissism and codependency. Yes, that's exactly it.

Another person brought up masking: neurodivergent people, people on the autism spectrum, and adults with ADHD masking to fit in. That would be survival. It's adaptive, a way to find a path to co-regulation. I would say it's the same kind of thing.

The same person described vulnerability in a way I loved. When we're vulnerable, our nervous system recognizes we need help, we need co-regulation, and it's reaching out. In the reaching out, we've dropped the mask. To receive the co-regulation, we have to let the other nervous system know, "I'm ready for an attachment moment." And we could be shunned. The word that describes that is vulnerable.

Someone wondered whether faking safety could have evolved, because acting like you like somebody can save you from a lot of immediate, physical pain, and deferring to authority feels like it comes from some old, root part of us.

I agree. I think we have something within us that naturally acquiesces to power. Look at the whole Will Smith thing at the Oscars, with Chris Rock. It was unbelievable. I was looking at everybody in the audience, and everyone was just kind of going along with it. I don't think they were confused, but no one spoke up. No one said, "Well, that wasn't right." Even Chris Rock had to kind of acquiesce.

Will Smith already was the most powerful person in that room, personality-wise, financially, in reach and influence. But he dominated that room and made himself the most powerful person there, and everyone else just fell in line, even though I'm sure they were worked up and activated. Could that be some kind of very old survival instinct? "Oh, everything's fine. I'm just here. No problems. Don't pay attention to me."

We take so many cues from the people around us. One person said that when she's feeling super activated in a room of people who aren't, she checks everybody's face, to decide whether it's just her or whether everyone is freaking out.
That's co-regulation. You're mindfully accepting co-regulation.

I do the same thing. When I do presentations, I have to see people's faces. During the pandemic, when I saw teachers doing the whole Zoom thing with black screens, I stepped into one of those classrooms for five minutes to do a presentation for the kids, and I was instantly like, "This is horrible. You can't see their faces? You're doing this for six hours a day? How are you staying sane?" It was dead quiet. It was eerie. So when I do Zooms now, I tell people I need to see their faces. I don't pressure them, but I let them know it would mean a lot. It makes such a big difference.
Someone brought up Brené Brown's idea that shame is the fear of disconnection.

The definitions we use are important. If that's accurately describing what she says about shame, to me, that's a fear of rejection and aloneness. I've conceptualized shame a different way. For me, shame is: I feel bad, I feel wrong, I feel defective. It's probably very much a dorsal vagal kind of thing, I think. And I think shame is oftentimes connected to disgust.

The fear of rejection, isolation, and aloneness could live on its own. They're often connected, but I would separate those two. I'm not saying I have the right answer. I'm just putting my thoughts out there.

I think there is a social function to shame. I don't want to say healthy shame. That doesn't fit right for me. Functional shame, social shame. Irene Lyon, when I interviewed her a long time ago, called it healthy shame as well. It feels icky to me, but I get it.

q: Healthy shame is teaching a child what's right from wrong. It's what needs to happen so that they stay safe.

blocks.p: Think of the few taboos that are close to universal across cultures: you don't smear poop on the walls, you don't have relations with your family members. Or, to be blatant: if there's a pedophile in the room, I want to know, so I can reject that person. There's a function to having lists of sexual offenders. It's icky. It feels gross. I know it destroys their life entirely, so maybe it's too far, I don't know. But it does serve a purpose for us. I have kids. Before we moved, I checked my neighborhood. I want to know. It's an alert. Shaming people is kind of an alert, as long as it's used in a functional way.

Shame can serve the function of, "Hey, you messed up so bad, you can no longer be a part of our system, our society, our family. You're out." In a well-regulated person, that could be enough of a consequence to say, "Oh, I better snap out of it and make some better choices here. I better make amends. I better give people plenty of space until I can do better." I'm talking very generally. There are probably some things that are unforgivable. I think there definitely are.

When well-regulated people, people who can connect with each other and have empathy, say, "Your behavior is intolerable. We are not okay with it. You have to go," that is shame. That is rejection. That is isolation. And I think there's a biological experience of that. If someone shames us, if someone rejects us, we feel it in a very deep way. That probably works in little tribes and families: "Hey, kick rocks. You don't belong in our tribe anymore." And then that person has to go live on their own, or find another tribe that's more accepting.

That's a heck of a lot different than continued shame, throwing rocks at people, bullying them online, people harassing each other and making fake Instagram accounts to spy on each other. It's just sick. I'm sorry I'm being judgmental here, but that's beyond the pale. That's your own shame that you're now inflicting on someone else who may not deserve it. Now they're left with shame that doesn't belong to them, but they've taken it on, and they might pass it on to someone else, harm somebody else, or harm themselves.

So I think there is a function to shame, from people who can give it in that regulated way, and hopefully the other person can receive it, learn their lesson, and do something different. I don't know if that's realistic. In the ideal idea of prison, I think that's the function: as a society, we're saying, "You don't belong here. You have to go over there." I don't think it works that way very often, but every now and then you hear about someone who says, "It took that for me to snap out of it and start repurposing my life in another direction."
Someone added that we've also always twisted shame to maintain power structures: racism, transphobia, the witches of Salem. Yep. Everything.
That led to a question about whether using time-outs as punishment is problematic. It can be. But I'll be honest, I've used time-out. It's pretty rare.

It depends on what we mean by time-out, and when I run parenting groups, this has to be cleared up. For me, time-out is very concrete. There's a structure to it. There are very clear boundaries around serious, zero tolerance behaviors: if you acted like this with your friends, they would reject you. They would say, "You cannot be a part of us anymore. Get out." To me, that's a natural consequence in the real world.

So if my son hits somebody, he's going to get a time-out, because in the real world I hope he has friends who will say, "Get lost." I hope my kids have friends who will not put up with that. A healthy friend is going to say, "Yo, that's way beyond. You cannot hang out with us right now. You cannot hit us. You cannot curse at us. You cannot treat us like this. That's not a part of our friendship." If my kids do anything that's a zero tolerance behavior my wife and I agree on, that results in a time-out. For my older kid, that would be more like a grounding.

That's different from what some parents call time-out. I've heard of parents putting their kids in a dark closet. That's not time-out. That's torture. I've heard of parents making their kids kneel on dry rice. That's abuse. That's torture. They call it time-out, but it's not. I've seen parents put their kids on time-out and say, "You're done when I tell you to," and the whole time they're shaming and humiliating the kid. That's not time-out.
So time-out, to me, is a very specific structure:

ul: There's a time to it. It is not unending.
Shame is not a part of it.
There is a piece of rejection in it. As social beings, I don't see a huge issue with that, as long as we're using it appropriately.
Afterward, there's a repair, a reattachment: "I love you. I expect the best out of you. Let's talk about the structure again. Let's problem solve."

blocks.p: One person who cares for young kids said it this way: a time-out can be about rejection, but not about abandonment. That's a heck of a lot different. She calls it "time to yourself." The child sits on the couch or in a chair away from her, but always somewhere they can see her. She doesn't talk to them or engage them, and depending on the child, she puts a clock on. Then they talk about it, restructure, and figure out how the child will do it differently next time. There's no shame in it. There's some rejection, but very little. And as she put it, the definition of discipline is to teach.

blocks.h: Why we can't sit with discomfort

blocks.p: The last big question was why it's so hard, as a society, to hold nuance. You've done a bad thing, you're ostracized.
I'd say sure, but then the next question is why. Why can we not sit with difficult ideas, and not just the ideas, but the discomfort that comes with them?

I was working with a young person who had some flat-out hateful and judgmental ideas, things I don't agree with. I knew that every time he talked about his ideas, he got judged, rejected, shamed, told, "No, that's not the right way to think." Just trying to correct his thoughts did not help. So my approach was to take him seriously. That doesn't mean I agreed with him. I told him, "I don't agree with you. But what I want to do in our sessions is give you an experience of not being judged. I want to give you an experience of being listened to. We're going to discuss, we might disagree, I might ask questions. Do the same thing with me."

But I had to be able to tolerate my own distress, because it is distressing. Inside, I was judging. I didn't say it out loud, but inside I'm going, "Whoa. No." You could feel that friction. Can I stay with that discomfort and then get to the nuance? Maybe he has some decent questions. Maybe where he's coming from is not judgment and hate. It definitely sounded like that, but there was more to it. There was more that rubbed him the wrong way, and then he targeted a group as the problem. That's obviously not the problem. But you have to be able to sit with your own discomfort to get there.

So back to the question: why can't we sit with discomfort? Ideas bring discomfort, and that discomfort is so intolerable for a lot of us now that we react instantly, with shaming, judgment, rejection. And I get it. I have it within me too, and that kind of scares me. If something were triggering enough, I could probably get to the point where I was misbehaving, and I don't want to be that person. I think we all have it within us.

Maybe it's always been this way. Somewhere along the line, I think we lost our natural ability to connect with each other, and we've just kind of existed in this traumatized state for I don't know how long. This shameful, traumatized state that we keep inflicting, generation after generation, constantly, across cultures and across the globe. I don't know where things got way off course. I wish I could pinpoint the moment in time when things got beyond the basic functioning of an organism. What was the first dysregulated organism? Was it human, or before humanity? I'm really curious.

Someone pointed out that we have neuroplasticity. The brain can change and adapt with new experience. It might take generations, but a person who isn't triggered all the time, raising a baby, a thousand times over, a million times over, ends up with a population better able to tolerate dysregulation. And the solution is probably more community-based. We need a community around us.
They also predicted there will be a cohort of very dysregulated humans as a result of the pandemic. I agree. What the heck is that going to look like? I don't know.
